newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian riot reveals tension and distrust.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian riot reveals tension and distrust.

text.p: The latest riots in West Java underscore a growing danger of Indonesians turning to violence in frustration over social problems, political and social analysts said on Friday.

A mob apparently incensed by a report of police brutality ran amok in Tasikmalaya on Thursday, burning and looting stores, homes and churches in an orgy of violence with racial and religious overtones.

As authorities deployed hundreds of troops to regain control of the town 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Jakarta, analysts said similar incidents would occur in the future because the government was not addressing the causes.
"The problem has to be seen in a wider context, we have to ask why violence becomes a way of solvin problems," sociologist Arief Budiman told Reuters.
"The democratic way of solving problems is blocked. The legal system does not work and when people negotiate, they always try to get a powerful group involved and use force," Budiman said.
"People do not trust the police, so they take problems into their own hands," he said.

Two ethnic Chinese died in the Tasikmalaya riot, which came less than three months after five Christians were burnt to death in church by a Moslem mob in Situbondo in East Java. In the earlier incident, 25 churches and a temple were attacked.

Police said the Tasikmalaya riot was apparently sparked by a report that police had beaten teachers from an Islamic school. Local news reports said one of the teachers had disciplined the son of a policeman, who summoned them for questioning.
In Situbondo, the mob started its rampage by destroying a court house where a Moslem heretic was on trial for blasphemy.
Analysts have noted the increasingly regular pattern on ethnic and religious violence in recent years throughout Indonesia.

Budiman said that with the government cracking down on groups that organise workers along class lines, religious solidarity is the only option for the masses in mostly Moslem Indonesia who feel marginalised by the country's rapid economic development.

"Christianity is also a symbol of wealth on Java and in western Indonesia, because Christians live in luxury, have a good educational system and have everything," said Budiman, an ethnic Chinese who is a Moslem.
"Whenever there is a riot, they cannot attack the government but they can attack the Chinese and the Christians," he said.
The head of the West Java military region Major-General Tayo Tamadi was quoted in the Moslem-run Republika daily on Friday as saying the riot was not a spontaneous action.
"It was three days since this incident first appeared," Tamadi said, apparently referring to the alleged police beating.
"Besides that, it can be seen from the targets of the disturbance that this is not something that came spontaneously from the crowd," he said.
Mochtor Buchori, a political commentator and former rector of a Jakarta Islamic university, said there was widespread frustration among Indonesia's nearly 200 million people.
"This is an expression of social and economic discontent, but it is probable there is someone directing the situation and exploiting it for political reasons," he said.

But Buchori said the community has been recently angered by a number of cases of reported police brutality, including a police raid on the minority Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) headquarters on July 27, which sparked widespread rioting in Jakarta.

Both Buchori and Budiman said police were regarded as generally corrupt and distrusted after they failed to properly investigate the suspicious murder in August of a Yoygakarta journalist who wrote critical articles about the government.
They said the widely publicised beating to death of a robbery suspect in police custody in Bogor was also important.
"We don't trust the government and the police any more and this lack of trust is a very destructive thing as it erodes our society," Buchori said, predicting more flare-ups in the future.
